title: Me and You
description: Say who you are and where you are from, ask someone's name, and point at yourself, the person in front of you and a third person with the right word. Your first sentences — with no verb 'to be' to worry about.
approach: GPA Phase 1 → 2 bridge. Self-introductions are heard from vloggers first, then the learner assembles their own with tap-to-build cards, then records it once.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 on the build-a-sentence quiz and one recorded self-introduction (unscored)
can_do: Say who you are and where you are from
Point at yourself, the listener and a third person with the right pronoun

grammar.title: أنا، إنت، إنتي، هو، هي — who is doing the talking
grammar.explanation: Five words cover almost every conversation: أنا (I), إنت (you, to a man), إنتي (you, to a woman), هو (he) and هي (she). The man/woman difference lives in the last vowel of 'you': inta versus inti. Egyptian has no separate polite 'you' like French vous — instead people say حضرتك ('your presence') to be respectful, which you will hear used on you. For a group, إحنا (we), إنتو (you all) and هم (they) are the same for men and women.

examples.english: Where are you from? (to a man)
Are you a student? (to a woman)

examples.arabic: هو من إسكندرية وهي من القاهرة
examples.transliteration: huwwa min iskindiriyya w-hiyya min el-qaahira
examples.english: He is from Alexandria and she is from Cairo

grammar.title: No word for 'is' or 'am'
grammar.explanation: To say 'I am a student', Egyptian just puts the two ideas side by side: أنا طالب — 'I student'. There is no 'am', 'is' or 'are' in the present. The same works with places (أنا من لندن, 'I from London') and names (اسمي سارة, 'my name Sara'). Yes/no questions are the same words with a rising voice: إنت طالب؟ 'you student?'. This is why your first sentences are so short — that is not baby talk, that is the grammar.

culture.title: Names, titles and what people will call you
culture.note: Egyptians use first names quickly, but almost always with a title in front: يا أستاذ أحمد for a man, يا مدام هدى for a married woman, يا آنسة for a young unmarried woman. Expect to be addressed as يا أستاذ or يا مدام yourself, and as يا باشا by taxi drivers and waiters — it is friendly flattery, not a rank. Parents are often called by their eldest child's name: أبو أحمد, أم أحمد. When you introduce yourself, say your name and where you are from and then ask back — the exchange is expected to be two-way.

phrases.english: Pleased to meet you (we are honoured)

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same everywhere in Arabic. Egyptians point at their own chest as they say it. It starts more sentences than any other word in this stage.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman pointing at her own chest with a light smile, plain background.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger introducing themselves to camera; أنا is the first word.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Written the same as the feminine but said inta. Egyptians write it إنت or انت. Used freely between equals; to a stranger or an elder, حضرتك is the softer choice.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing an open hand at another man in front of him.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviewers turning a question on a man; وإنت؟ at the end of an answer.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same word as إنت with the final vowel changed to i — the pattern you met in إزيك / إزيكي. Often written إنتي to make the difference visible.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing an open hand at another woman in front of her.

example.english: Where are you from? (to a woman)

vocabulary.video_hint: An interviewer addressing a woman; the final -i is audible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said huwwa with a doubled w in Cairo — not the two-letter huwa of the textbook. Also used for 'it' when the thing is masculine.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing sideways at a man standing a little apart, who is looking away.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone introducing a third person; a finger or open hand toward them.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said hiyya with a doubled y. Also 'it' for feminine things — which is most words ending in ة, so you will hear it about cars and cups as well as people.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing sideways at a woman standing a little apart, who is smiling at the camera.
vocabulary.video_hint: Introducing a woman in a group; family vlogs naming a sister or friend.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Rarely heard bare — almost always with an ending: اسمي (my name), اسمك (your name), اسمه (his name), اسمها (her name). Learn it as the root of those four.
vocabulary.image_scene: A blank name badge on a lanyard with a pen beside it, 'name' implied by the badge outline.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone giving or asking a name; a badge or a form on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: اسم + the ending -i (my). Egyptians say اسمي X, or simply أنا X. The ending -i is the same 'my' you will put on every family word in the next lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a hand on his chest, a speech bubble showing a name badge with a heart on it.

example.english: My name is Sara — and you?

vocabulary.video_hint: The first line of a self-introduction to camera.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'your name what?' — the question word comes at the end, where the answer will go. To a woman: اسمك إيه (ismik eeh), written اسمكِ or اسمك. Never ما اسمك — that is a textbook.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman asking a boy his name at a school gate, leaning down with a smile.

example.english: What's your name, dear? (to a child)

vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews opening with the name question; a teacher asking a child.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The same word as MSA and every dialect. Short: min. It glues onto the place name: من مصر, من لندن.
vocabulary.image_scene: An arrow leaving a map pin marked with a small house icon, pointing outward.
vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone saying where they are from; a map or city name on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two words and you have said where you are from — no verb needed. Egyptians will usually follow up with the neighbourhood: من القاهرة؟ منين في القاهرة؟
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman pointing at herself, then at a country outlined on a map behind her.
vocabulary.video_hint: A foreigner on camera saying where they are from; interviewers asking منين.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'a happy occasion'. Reply: أنا أسعد ('I am happier'). The more formal تشرفنا ('we are honoured') is also common, answered with الشرف ليا. Either is fine; you will hear both.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two people shaking hands for the first time, both smiling, a third person introducing them.
vocabulary.video_hint: First-meeting handshakes; often followed by أنا أسعد.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A woman is طالبة (ṭaliba — the long aa shortens when the ending is added). Plural طلبة. Useful because it answers the second question every Egyptian asks: what do you do?
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a backpack and a notebook outside a university gate.

example.english: I am a student at the university

vocabulary.video_hint: University campus interviews; someone saying أنا طالب.

vocabulary.teaching_note: من (from) + فين (where) squeezed into one word. It is the question that follows your name within seconds. Answer with أنا من….
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a puzzled, friendly look pointing at a stranger, a question mark over a map.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews; the question right after the name.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A woman is مصرية (maṣriyya). Note مصر means both Egypt and, for people outside the capital, Cairo. Nationalities follow the same pattern: أمريكي، إنجليزي، ألماني.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man in a plain shirt with a small Egyptian flag pin, the Nile and a bridge behind him.
vocabulary.video_hint: People stating nationality or hometown; the flag or a Cairo landmark in shot.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'your presence'. Use it instead of إنت with anyone older, a shopkeeper, an official. It stands alone with no يا. To a woman: حضرتكِ (ḥaḍritik). Being called حضرتك is a compliment.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man speaking to an older gentleman in a suit, hand slightly raised in respect.
vocabulary.video_hint: Formal or service exchanges; a younger speaker addressing an older one.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: Hi, my name is Sara. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.english: I'm Tom. Nice to meet you

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: أنا أسعد. إنت منين يا توم؟
dialogue.transliteration: ana asʿad. inta mineen ya tom?
dialogue.english: Likewise. Where are you from, Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: أنا مصرية من القاهرة. إنت طالب؟
dialogue.transliteration: ana maṣriyya min el-qaahira. inta ṭaalib?
dialogue.english: I'm Egyptian, from Cairo. Are you a student?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.arabic: أيوه، أنا طالب. وهو كمان طالب
dialogue.transliteration: aywa, ana ṭaalib. w-huwwa kamaan ṭaalib
dialogue.english: Yes, I'm a student. And he is a student too

sound_spotlight.explanation: One vowel carries the whole difference between talking to a man and a woman. Egyptians hear it instantly; practise saying the pair back to back until the last vowel is clean.

sound_spotlight.sound: Doubled و and ي in هو، هي
sound_spotlight.explanation: Cairo doubles the middle consonant: huw-wa, hiy-ya. The textbook huwa/hiya sounds foreign. Hold the w and y a beat longer than feels natural.
You learned that ق is usually a throat-catch (قهوة → ʾahwa). In a handful of formal words — القاهرة, القرآن — Egyptians keep the deep q. The name of the city is the one you need now; hear it with q.
A rasp at the back of the mouth, like the ch in Scottish 'loch'. You have been hearing it since صباح الخير; from here on try producing it — a soft k with the throat open is close enough.

lesson_sequence.detail: A university gate in Cairo, students passing. One line of English: today you say who you are, where you are from, and ask the same back. Tap يلا.
Three short self-introductions from three speakers (a Cairo student, an Alexandrian woman, a foreigner). Arabic on screen; the learner taps the name and the place as they hear them.
أنا، إنت، إنتي، هو، هي as cards with a pointing illustration each. Audio; then a tap game: a voice says a pronoun, the learner taps the person it points at.
Tap-to-build: cards أنا / اسمي / من / مصري / طالب plus the learner's own name and country appear; drag them into two sentences. Audio plays the result.
The learner hears اسمك إيه؟ and إنت منين؟ and taps the matching answer; then hears the answer and taps the matching question.
Say your own introduction: name, where from, student or not. Recorded, played back, not scored. Optional retake.
Twelve build-a-sentence items. Counter rolls to 56 words. Nudge: introduce yourself in Egyptian to someone this week.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Introduce yourself to an Arabic speaker today in one breath: أنا [name]، أنا من [place]. Then ask وإنت؟
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. First real production of a two-sentence turn.

real_world_prompts.prompt: When someone asks your name this week, answer with اسمي … even if they asked in English.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Automates the -i ending on اسم.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor to introduce three imaginary people using هو and هي and point at the pictures; you say back who is who.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Third-person pronouns in a recognition game.

queries: اسمك إيه ومنين إنت مقابلات شارع
